text: Motion in 2D and 3D. Chapter Roadmap. This chapter extends one-dimensional kinematics into two and three dimensions. Position, displacement, velocity and acceleration are now treated as vectors, but the basic ideas from Chapter 3 still apply component by component. As you read, focus on three questions. Item 1. Can I break a vector motion problem into independent components? Item 2. Can I identify which quantities are shared between the component motions? Item 3. Can I recombine components to describe the full motion of an object? These ideas will be used to analyze projectile motion, circular motion and relative motion. Displacement and velocity vectors. Displacement vector. To describe motion in 2D and 3D, we must first define a coordinate system, including a convention of axes. Recall that the sign of the acceleration due to gravity was determined by the convention that we chose. We usually use the Cartesian coordinate system to locate a particle at point P x, y, z in three dimensions. If the particle is moving, the variables x, y, z are functions of time, t. The position vector, vector r of t, locates the point P at a time t from the origin by vector r of t equals x of t i hat plus y of t j hat plus z of t k. Figure referenced in the course notes. Shows the position vector, vector r of t, for a particle located at a time t. Note that the orientation of the coordinate system follows the right hand rule. Checkpoint. If vector r of t sub 1 and vector r of t sub 2 are both measured from the origin, why does change in vector r point from the first position to the second position rather than the first position? We can now define the 3D displacement vector change in vector r as the difference between the position vector, vector r of t sub 2 at time t sub 2 and the initial position vector, vector r of t sub 1 at time t sub 1. Or change in vector r equals vector r of t sub 2 minus vector r of t sub 1. 3D vector addition is performed in the same way as in 2d by adding the corresponding components or graphically by using the head to tail method, figure referenced in the course notes. See the Python code below that demonstrates how to plot a 3D vector in map plot lib. See the Python snippet given in the course lecture notes. MIT OpenCourseWare. Example problem. Polar orbiting satellite. The problem. A satellite is in a circular polar orbit around Earth at an altitude of 400 kilometers, meaning it passes directly over the north and south poles. What are the magnitude and direction of the displacement vector from when the satellite is directly over the north pole to when it is at latitude negative 45 degrees? The model. The satellite is modeled as a point moving along a circular polar orbit around Earth. The displacement is not the distance traveled along the orbit, it is the straight line vector from the initial position to the final position. The origin is placed at the center of Earth with plus j hat pointing north and plus i hat toward the equator on the side of the orbit. With this coordinate choice, the satellite starts directly over the north pole and ends at latitude negative 45 degrees. The math. The position vectors are measured from the center of Earth, so the orbital radius is the sum of Earth's radius, 6,370 kilometers, and the satellite altitude. R equals 6,370 kilometers, plus 400 kilometers equals 6,770 kilometers. At the north pole position, the satellite lies entirely along the positive y direction. Vector R1 equals 6,770 j hat kilometers. At latitude negative 45 degrees, the position vector is resolved into components using the latitude angle measured from the equatorial direction in the orbital plane. Vector R2 equals R cosine negative 45 degrees i hat plus R sine negative 45 degrees j hat. Substituting the orbital radius into the component form gives the final position vector. Vector R2 equals 4,790 i hat minus 4,790 j hat kilometers. The displacement vector is found by subtracting the initial position vector from the final position vector. Change in vector R equals vector R2 minus vector R1 equals 4,790 i hat minus 4,790 j hat kilometers. Minus 6,770 j hat kilometers. Equals 4,790 i hat minus 1.16 times 10 to the 4 j hat kilometers. The magnitude of the displacement is found from the Pythagorean theorem applied to the vector components. Magnitude of change in vector R equals the square root of 4,790 squared plus negative 1.16 times 10 to the 4 squared kilometers. Equals 1.25 times 10 to the 4 kilometers. The direction is found from the inverse tangent of the y component divided by the x component. Fata equals tan to the power of negative 1. Fraction negative 1.16 times 10 to the 4 over 4,790 equals negative 67.5 degrees. The negative angle means the displacement points below the positive x axis or 67.5 degrees south of east. The conclusion. The displacement from the north pole position to the latitude negative 45 degrees position is change in vector R equals 47,90 i hat minus 1.16 times 10 to the 4 j hat kilometers. Its magnitude is 1.25 times 10 to the 4 kilometers and it points 67.5 degrees south of east. This is a straight line displacement between the two positions, not the distance traveled along the circular orbit. The problem. The position function of a particle is vector R of t equals 2.0 t squared i hat plus 2.0 plus 3.0 t j hat plus 5.0 k hat kilometers. A. What is the instantaneous velocity vector and speed at t equals 2.0 seconds? B. What is the average velocity between t equals 1.0 seconds and t equals 3.0 seconds? The model. The particle moves in three-dimensional Cartesian coordinates. Instantaneous velocity is found from the rate of change of the position vector, while average velocity over a finite interval is found from the displacement during that interval divided by the elapsed time. Each component can be evaluated independently and then recombined into a vector. Because the x position is quadratic in time and the y and z positions are linear in time, only the x component of velocity changes with time. The math. The instantaneous velocity is defined as the time derivative of the position vector. V of t equals d vector R over dt. Differentiating the position function component by component gives the velocity function. Vector V of t equals 4.0 t i hat plus 3.0 j hat plus 5.0 k hat kilometers per second. A. The instantaneous velocity at t equals 2.0 seconds is found by substituting that time into the velocity function. Vector V of 2.0 equals 8.0 i hat plus 3.0 j hat plus 5.0 k hat kilometers per second. The speed is the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity vector. Magnitude of vector V of 2.0 equals square root of 8.0 squared plus 3.0 squared plus 5.0 squared kilometers per second equals 9.9 kilometers per second. B. The average velocity over the interval from t1 equals 1.0 seconds to t2 equals 3.0 seconds is the displacement divided by the elapsed time. Vector V of equals vector R of t2 minus vector R of t1 over t2 minus t1. The endpoint position vectors are found by substituting both times into the position function. Vector R of 1.0 equals 2.0 i hat plus 5.0 j hat plus 5.0 k hat kilometers. Vector R of 3.0 equals 18.0 i hat plus 11.0 j hat plus 15.0 k hat kilometers. The displacement is found by subtracting the first endpoint from the second endpoint. Vector R of 3.0 minus vector R of 1.0 equals 16.0 i hat plus 6.0 j hat plus 10.0 k hat kilometers. Dividing this displacement by the elapsed time gives the average velocity. Vector V of equals 16.0 i hat plus 6.0 j hat plus 10.0 k hat kilometers over 2.0 seconds equals 8.0 i hat plus 3.0 j hat plus 5.0 k hat kilometers. Vector R of t1 minus vector R of 1.0 is found by subtracting the first endpoint from the first endpoint. Vector R of t1 minus vector R of 1.0 equals 16.0. After that, you can substitute a specific value like t equals 2.0 using dot subs t comma 2.0 and convert to a float with float of dot dot dot. This is especially useful when Vector R of t is complicated and you want to avoid algebra mistakes. The conclusion. At t equals 2.0 seconds, the instantaneous velocity is Vector V of 2.0 equals 8.0 i hat plus 3.0 j hat plus 5.0 k hat kilometers per second. The speed is 9.9 kilometers per second. The average velocity between 1.0 seconds and 3.0 seconds is also 8.0 i hat plus 3.0 j hat plus 5.0 k hat kilometers per second. In this interval, the average velocity equals the instantaneous velocity at the midpoint because the velocity is a linear function of time.
